item.title: QuFrame: Pauli Frame Tracking for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Control
item.description:
Skim new method — QuFrame closes the QEC feedback loop within a 1 µs round budget with fallback decoding in 144 ns, cutting the logical error rate by an average of 38.5% compared to a serialized blocking baseline.

Grade 0.540 · 2.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum error correction with silicon spin qubits” · Aleksandra Świerkowska, Ilgaz Er, Emmanouil Giortamis, Pramod Bhatotia

Figure

Logical error rate versus physical error rate scaling factor for a rotated surface code (d=3, 9 rounds). QuFrame avoids stalling and tracks closest to the ideal zero-latency baseline, outperforming the serialized blocking controller across all noise levels.

Asks

How can a quantum controller track the Pauli frame in real time with bounded per-instruction latency under multi-core dispatch and decoders of variable latency?

Before

A serialized blocking controller, as modeled in XQsim (Byun et al., 2022), increased logical error rates by up to 4.1× over an ideal zero-latency controller.

But

Evaluated on a distance-3 rotated surface code with 17 physical qubits; IBM Heron coherence times prolonged 10× in simulations; fallback lookup table memory scales poorly for higher code distances without truncation.

Tools

QuFrameISA · Instruction Resolution Engine (IRE) · Pauli Frame Management Unit (versioned compare-and-swap) · AMD Alveo V80 FPGA · Helios simulator with IBM Heron noise model

Abstract

Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires continuous quantum error correction (QEC) to suppress physical noise. While Clifford-only workloads can defer corrections to software post-processing, universal computation breaks this paradigm: executing non-Clifford gates via magic-state gadgets introduces hard, real-time control-flow dependencies on error-corrected measurements. Consequently, the controller must extract syndromes, decode them, and update the Pauli frame in real time, closing the entire QEC loop within a strict 1 μs cycle. However, prior proposals on Pauli frame tracking remain largely theoretical, leaving the microarchitectural bottlenecks of tracking, resolving, and synchronizing frame updates across distributed control pipelines unaddressed. To this end, we present QuFrame, a control microarchitecture for real-time Pauli frame tracking that closes the QEC loop within 1 μs while sustaining QPU-rate throughput. By introducing QuFrameISA, we cleanly decouple instruction execution from continuous Pauli frame management. Execution is distributed across per-qubit Instruction Resolution Engines (IREs) that resolve instructions against the frame via a single table lookup, while a Pauli Frame Management Unit enables independent, lock-free concurrent commits. To strictly guarantee the 1 μs deadline, QuFrame pairs an asynchronous primary decoder with an on-chip fallback decoder that resolves in 144 ns, natively reconciling divergent updates in hardware without degrading logical error rates.

item.title: Fault-tolerant quantum processor with minimal external control
item.description:
Skim theory — Universal fault-tolerant quantum computation requires only a constant number (le20) of external control wires on an n-qubit chip, executing n/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀(n/ϵ) logical qubits with depth-3 periodic geometrically local operations.

Grade 0.552 · 3.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Christopher A. Pattison, Jeongwan Haah, John Preskill

Figure

Unrolling of a 1D brickwork quantum circuit into a 2D tile where qubits propagate continuously upward across a physical planar lattice.

Asks

How much external control is strictly necessary to operate a fault-tolerant universal quantum processor?

But

Asymptotic analysis. Assumes a noiseless global clock and physical noise on all operations below a universal positive constant. Logical gate time is n/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀(n/ϵ) without instantaneous classical wires.

Tools

spacetime unrolling into 2D tiles · concatenated quantum codes · periodic depth-3 cellular automata · fault-tolerant instruction decoding

Abstract

Contemporary classical information processors integrate tens of billions of transistors printed on a chip, yet are fully controlled through comparatively few external wires. This is possible because data flows through hard-coded operations in step with a global clock and is steered by external instructions. Today's solid-state quantum processors are different -- every qubit receives instructions from outside the chip via its own dedicated control line, and error correction adds a further torrent of syndrome data that is transported off-chip. Here we show that the external control of a quantum chip can be greatly simplified. We propose a fault-tolerant architecture for universal quantum computation, inspired by modern classical processors, in which quantum information flows through a fixed, clocked device, propelled by local gates in a planar array. Our quantum processor receives an input stream of classical instructions via a small, constant number of external wires, each attached to a single qubit. Except for those few qubits coupled to external wires, all qubits evolve under a periodically-applied geometrically-local depth-3 circuit, which is fixed at the time the device is fabricated. Assuming a noiseless global clock (so that every operation is applied on schedule, though imperfectly), we establish an accuracy threshold theorem: For physical noise below a universal threshold -- afflicting every gate, measurement, and wire -- a chip with n physical qubits can run any quantum algorithm that uses~n/sfpolylog(n/ε) logical qubits, where ε is the error rate per logical gate. Each logical gate takes time~n/sfpolylog(n/ε); an alternative design, in which quantum operations remain strictly local and noisy, but on-chip wires broadcast noiseless classical signals instantaneously, reduces the time per logical gate to sfpolylog(n/ε).

item.title: High-rate low-distance color codes
item.description:
Skim new result — Two-dimensional color codes reach optimal encoding rates of 1/3 at distance 3 and 1/4 at distance 4. In a linear ion chain model, simulated [[20,4,4]] and [[16,4,4]] codes hit break-even at two-qubit gate infidelities of 0.22% and 0.26%.

Grade 0.516 · 2.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Peter-Jan H. S. Derks, Lucas Berent, Mark Webster, Robert Wille, Jens Eisert, Aleksander Kubica

Figure

Break-even two-qubit gate infidelity plotted against total qubits required per QEC cycle across distance-3 and distance-4 2D color codes. Shows [[16,4,4]] and [[20,4,4]] breaking even above 2×10−3 physical error rate using 36 to 46 qubits.

Asks

What are the optimal encoding rates for small, low-distance 2D color codes, and can they achieve break-even performance in trapped-ion chains?

Before

Bivariate bicycle codes with weight-5 stabilizers required [[30,4,5]] and [[48,4,7]] implementations with Shor-style extraction (Wang et al. 2024).

But

Numerical simulation only. Holds strictly for color codes with only color boundaries on surfaces with Euler characteristic χ≥0.

Tools

Steane-style error correction · Linear trapped-ion chain circuit-level noise model · Real-time feedback without post-selection · Tesseract / lookup-table decoding

Code. https://github.com/peter-janderks/small_color_codes

Abstract

Experimental implementations of two-dimensional color codes encoding a single logical qubit have surpassed the fidelity of physical qubits. A natural next step is to investigate higher-rate codes that encode multiple logical qubits. Here we propose small, high-rate 2D color codes for this purpose. We design distance-3 codes with encoding rates up to 1/3 and distance-4 codes with encoding rates up to 1/4. We prove that these rates are optimal for color codes with only color boundaries on surfaces with non-negative Euler characteristic. We benchmark the codes by simulating Steane-style error correction with real-time feedback and no post-selection in a linear trapped-ion chain model with all-to-all connectivity. The two best-performing codes have parameters [[20,4,4]] and [[16,4,4]] and achieve break-even at two-qubit gate infidelities of 0.22% and 0.26%, respectively. These results match the performance of Shor-style error correction with bivariate bicycle codes that use weight-5 measurements.

item.title: Singlet flags: using native entanglement to restore the circuit distance of shuttled qLDPC codes in silicon
item.description:
Skim new method — Using a stationary entangled singlet partner to flag bit flips on a shuttled ancilla restores circuit distance from 1-4 up to 5 or 6 on weight-8 and weight-10 codes, raising the Gross code [[144,12,12]] circuit distance from 7 to 10 in both bases.

Grade 0.506 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · William Chow, Jonathan Baugh

Figure

Logical error rate per round versus physical error rate p for distance-6 codes of weights 6, 8, and 10 decoded via BP+OSD and exact integer programming. Exact decoding reveals gains of up to 70x-90x over CAbLECAR that BP+OSD underreports.

Asks

Can preparing a mobile shuttling ancilla as part of an entangled spin singlet catch propagating hook errors and restore circuit distance in qLDPC syndrome extraction?

Before

CAbLECAR mobile ancillas kept only three-eighths to three-quarters of code distance, falling to circuit distance 1 at check weight 12.

But

Circuit-level Pauli noise model only, shuttling routing uses heuristic schedules, and exact distances are schedule-dependent.

Tools

singlet-flag syndrome extraction · circuit-level Pauli noise simulation · exact integer-program decoding via HiGHS · BP+OSD decoding

Abstract

High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes could greatly reduce the qubit count of silicon spin-qubit processors, but their checks are long-range and of high weight. Shuttling one ancilla electron through every data qubit of a check measures such checks, but a single fault on the ancilla spreads to several data qubits, so the circuit distance can fall far below the code distance. We make the mobile ancilla one half of a spin singlet whose partner stays at home; a Bell measurement at the end of the check provides a flag for isolated bit-flip faults acquired during the walk. Using new distance-6 codes with check weights 8, 10 and 12, and exact circuit distances from two independent solvers, we show that without the flag the circuit distance falls as check weight grows, to 1 at weight 12, while with it every weight-8 and weight-10 code recovers circuit distance 5 or 6 and corrects as many faults as the code. For codes of distance 8 to 12 the flag raises the circuit distance by one to four, and the Gross code [[144,12,12]] rises from 7 to 10. In circuit-level simulations of shuttled spin qubits, the flag lowers logical error rates by typically 2-10x across bivariate-bicycle, circulant-permutation and surface codes, and the gain survives percent-level flag-readout errors and bit flips on the singlet's electrons. BP+OSD does not reach the full circuit distance of the flagged circuits, so our flagged logical error rates are upper bounds: decoding the same shots exactly raises the flag's gain on the distance-6 codes from 3-7x to 5-17x for the weight-6 BB code, and from 1-12x to 5-90x at weights 8 and 10 for p >= 2.5x10^-4.
